items.title: Sol Yaged interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000
items.q: I played with him occasionally... I worked at Eddie Condon’s or I worked at Nick’s in the Village.

ctx.x: A very fine gentleman. A wonderful man, a wonderful pianist, and one of the highlights of my career because I knew about his music with Benny Goodman and he actually took me under his wing. He was very nice to me, and very warm and gracious to me. And every time I played with Fletcher Henderson I was thinking about the days that Benny Goodman was playing his music. “King Porter Stomp,” “Wrapping it Up,” “Stealing Apples,” “Dear Old Southland.” And when I played with him I felt like I was in my glory. He’s a…
What about working with, you know I hear an awful lot of stories about Eddie Condon.

I played with him occasionally, you know, I wasn’t the number one clarinet player with him, I’ll be very honest with you. The number one clarinetist was Pee Wee Russell. And then when Pee Wee Russell wasn’t able to make it they used Tony Parenti, a wonderful Dixieland clarinetist from New Orleans. And then they used other musicians, a clarinet player that worked with him for a while was Peanuts Hucko, a wonderful clarinetist.
